chapter_title: School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy
learning_objective: The learner will classify eight events from the history of schooling and educational technology into one of five eras, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: timeline **sim-id:** schooling-edtech-timeline
**Library:** vis-timeline
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** classify
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify eight events from the history of schooling and educational technology into one of five eras, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** the industrial-era school model, Carnegie unit, education policy, charter school, virtual school, history of EdTech (all defined in this chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** After exploring the timeline, the learner is shown eight events without dates and assigns each to one of five eras. An assignment is correct when it matches the "Correct era" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Exploring the timeline is not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Technology in schools is a recent phenomenon. (2) Every wave of educational technology was adopted quickly and used as promised. (3) School structures such as the Carnegie unit and age grading came from the computer age. **Instructional Rationale:** Placing events in eras requires the learner to organize them into a sequence and see how structures, policies, and technologies interleave, rather than memorizing dates. **Content:** Five eras: | Era | Years | |---|---| | 1 | 1840 to 1909 | | 2 | 1910 to 1959 | | 3 | 1960 to 1989 | | 4 | 1990 to 2009 | | 5 | 2010 to present | Events shown on the timeline, in three groups (Structure, Policy, Technology), each with a one-sentence description shown on selection: | Year | Group | Event | Description shown | |---|---|---|---| | 1848 | Structure | Quincy Grammar School opens | Usually cited as the first age-graded school in the United States. | | 1906 | Structure | Carnegie unit defined | 120 hours of class time in one subject becomes the standard high school credit. | | 1913 | Technology | Edison predicts film will replace textbooks | Thomas Edison is reported to have predicted that motion pictures would make textbooks obsolete in schools. | | 1924 | Technology | Pressey's testing machine | A machine that gave multiple-choice questions and advanced only on correct answers. | | 1954 | Policy | Brown v. Board of Education | The Supreme Court rules racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional. | | 1954 | Technology | Skinner's teaching machine | B. F. Skinner proposes machines that give immediate feedback in small steps. | | 1956 | Technology | Hagerstown closed-circuit television | Washington County, Maryland, tests televised lessons across many classrooms. | | 1960 | Technology | PLATO launched | The University of Illinois begins a computer-based instruction system. | | 1965 | Policy | Elementary and Secondary Education Act | Title I funding for schools serving low-income students begins. | | 1975 | Policy | Education for All Handicapped Children Act | Students with disabilities are guaranteed a free, appropriate public education; later renamed IDEA. | | 1977 | Technology | Apple II reaches schools | Microcomputers begin to appear in classrooms. | | 1991 | Policy | First charter school law | Minnesota passes the first law allowing charter schools. | | 1996 | Technology | E-rate program | The Telecommunications Act creates a subsidy for school internet access. | | 1997 | Structure | Florida Virtual School begins | One of the first state-run virtual schools. | | 2002 | Policy | No Child Left Behind | Annual testing and accountability for results become federal law. | | 2008 | Technology | Khan Academy becomes a nonprofit | Free online video lessons and practice reach a mass audience. | | 2013 | Technology | Los Angeles iPad rollout | A large district launches a one-to-one device program that soon runs into problems. | | 2015 | Policy | Every Student Succeeds Act | Much accountability authority returns to the states. | | 2020 | Structure | Emergency remote learning | School closures in March move nearly all schools online. | | 2022 | Technology | ChatGPT released | A general-purpose AI chatbot reaches the public on November 30. | Eight events for the classification task: | # | Event shown (no date) | Correct era | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Carnegie unit defined | 1 | It was defined in 1906. | | 2 | Pressey's testing machine | 2 | It was built in 1924. | | 3 | Hagerstown closed-circuit television | 2 | The experiment began in 1956. | | 4 | Elementary and Secondary Education Act | 3 | It was enacted in 1965. | | 5 | Education for All Handicapped Children Act | 3 | It was enacted in 1975. | | 6 | Florida Virtual School begins | 4 | It began in 1997. | | 7 | No Child Left Behind | 4 | It became law in 2002. | | 8 | Los Angeles iPad rollout | 5 | It was launched in 2013. | **Provenance:** Dates and events come from the chapter sections "The Industrial-Era School Model," "Education Policy, School Boards, and Standardized Testing," "Alternatives to the Traditional School," and "The History of Educational Technology." Dates should be verified against primary sources before the sim is published. **Rules:** An event belongs to the era whose years include its year, inclusive at both ends. The timeline can be filtered by group (Structure, Policy, Technology). Zoom and pan are available by buttons; mouse-wheel zoom is disabled. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner explores the timeline, selecting events to read their descriptions and filtering by group. 2. The learner starts the classification. One event appears at a time without its date. 3. The learner assigns the event to an era and submits. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text. 4. After all 8 events, the sim shows the score and the misplaced events with their dates. 5. The learner should notice that technology events cluster in the last three eras, while the structures they run into were set in the first. **Feedback:** 8 events, shuffled once per session, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: era [n]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text]." The correct era is revealed after the attempt. A running score "n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can place the major moments in schooling history." For a score < 7: "Explore the timeline again and retry; the events will be reshuffled." **Starting State:** The full timeline of 20 events is shown across all three groups, with no event selected, and the prompt reads "How long have schools been promised a technology revolution?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter names the dates 1848, 1906, 1913, 1924, 1954, 1956, 1960, 1965, 1975, 1977, 1991, 1996, 1997, 2002, 2008, 2012, 2013, 2015, 2020, and 2022. The timeline is a subset of these dates and must agree with them.
